strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely robustness problem for camera-based BEV 3D detectors in autonomous driving: non-contact adversarial 3D objects that can suppress nearby vehicle detections.
weaknesses: The central physical/deployability claims are not fully supported. The attack is evaluated by digital rendering onto nuScenes images, with simplified lighting/material modeling and occlusion estimated from 2D projected boxes plus SAM2 masks rather than true scene geometry. This makes it unclear whether the learned meshes would remain effective as real physical objects under illumination, sensor noise, shadows, motion blur, scale changes, and camera exposure effects.

strengths: The paper addresses an important robustness question for camera-based BEV 3D detection: whether a nearby, non-contact 3D object can suppress vehicle detections across calibrated multi-view inputs.
weaknesses: The central real-world/deployability claim is not well supported. All evidence appears to be digital insertion into nuScenes frames, with no physical experiment, no printability/material constraints, no lighting/camera-domain study, and no evaluation under real sensor capture. The method also depends on accurate calibration, 3D annotations, and SAM-based occlusion masks, which makes the threat model much less practical than the paper suggests.

The evaluation baseline is weak. Adv3D is the only main comparator, and the comparison is not clearly controlled: the initial NDS/mAP differs substantially between methods, and the paper does not compare against simpler 3D object insertion, textured distractors, random/optimized 2D patches, or non-adversarial objects of similar size and placement.

The metrics and interpretation are concerning. ASR is defined relative to detections after inserting the initialized object rather than the clean model, while the initialized object itself already degrades performance. This makes it hard to isolate adversarial optimization from ordinary occlusion, distribution shift, or rendered-object artifacts.

The claimed generality is overstated. Random placement performs poorly for a single mesh and only becomes strong when many meshes are inserted, which is a much less subtle and less realistic scenario. The limitations section itself notes poor robustness to target-position changes and weaker behavior on BEVDet4D.

The method is not technically crisp enough. Several equations and descriptions are underspecified or inconsistent, e.g. the occlusion depth test appears to contain a typo, the localization loss is written as an unbounded negative L1 term, texture/geometry constraints are barely specified, and the role/weights of the feature-similarity loss are not ablated.

Ablations are limited. The paper studies shape and distance, but does not isolate the proposed BEV spatial feature loss, vertex optimization versus texture-only optimization, SAM occlusion processing, placement strategy, object size, visibility, number of target vehicles, or attack transfer under matched conditions.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as exact target selection, optimization schedule, mesh constraints, texture parameterization, loss implementation for different detector heads, evaluation filtering, and whether code/models will be released are not sufficiently specified.

Presentation has multiple clarity issues and overclaims. The manuscript repeatedly uses terms such as universal, realistic, physically plausible, deployable, and critical flaws, but the reported experiments mainly demonstrate white-box digital vulnerability under favorable insertion conditions. There are also noticeable grammatical and formatting artifacts.

strengths: The paper studies an important and timely robustness problem for camera-based BEV 3D detectors: whether a non-contact, spatially consistent 3D object can suppress nearby vehicle predictions. This is a meaningful threat model distinct from vehicle camouflage or 2D pasted patches.

The proposed pipeline is conceptually coherent: mesh placement in 3D, differentiable multi-view rendering, approximate occlusion handling, and BEV feature-guided optimization. The 3D consistency across camera views and temporal inputs is a useful contribution relative to less geometrically grounded baselines.

The empirical evidence is fairly broad for a paper of this type. Results are reported on nuScenes with BEVDet, BEVDet4D, and BEVFormer; the attack reduces NDS/mAP substantially, and the appendix includes transfer experiments across victim models.
The paper includes relevant ablations over mesh shape, target distance, random placement, and occlusion handling. These help clarify when the attack is strongest and where it weakens.

The comparison to Adv3D is useful: the proposed method appears to preserve more scene integrity while achieving targeted vehicle suppression, which supports the claimed value of the non-invasive formulation.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about deployability and real-world physical plausibility are not fully supported. All evidence appears to be simulation/rendering-based; there is no physical print/manufacture test, no real camera capture, and limited treatment of lighting/material mismatch, motion blur, weather, shadows, or sensor exposure effects.

The attack uses privileged information in several places: target 3D boxes for placement, annotated scene objects for occlusion reasoning, calibrated multi-view geometry, and white-box model access for optimization. This is acceptable as a robustness probe, but the paper sometimes frames the threat as more practical than the evaluated setting demonstrates.

The occlusion module is approximate and may depend on ground-truth annotations and SAM2 masks at evaluation time. It uses projected 2D boxes and minimum-depth heuristics rather than true scene depth, so claims of realistic occlusion should be softened or better validated.

The evaluation would be stronger with ablations isolating each loss term in the BEV spatial feature-guided objective, especially the scene-confusion term. Current results show the full method works but do not clearly identify which optimization components are necessary.

The definition of ASR relative to detections with the initialized object rather than the clean scene makes interpretation less direct. Since the initialized object itself changes NDS/mAP and prediction locations, the attack success partly depends on a shifted baseline.

Generalization is mixed. The paper reports transfer results, but also acknowledges poor suppression under random placement and weaker performance on BEVDet4D. This limits the universality claim, especially for moving-agent scenarios where relative placement changes naturally.

The baseline comparison is somewhat narrow. Adv3D is relevant, but additional comparisons or adapted non-invasive/patch-based BEV attacks would help establish whether the gain comes from 3D consistency, mesh optimization, placement strategy, or simply using a nearby rendered object.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Some implementation details are provided, but important choices such as exact train/validation target selection, object material/lighting setup, texture parameterization, optimization schedules, and code availability are unclear.

The manuscript needs polish: there are formatting artifacts such as 'e.glet@tokeneonedot', equation/text typos, crowded tables, and some grammatical issues. These are presentation problems rather than core scientific flaws, but they do reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting and timely threat model for BEV perception: non-invasive 3D adversarial objects placed in the environment rather than on the target vehicle. This is a meaningful direction because it better matches scene-level manipulation risks than many prior patch/camouflage attacks.

The method is technically coherent: it combines 3D mesh insertion through calibrated rendering, an occlusion-aware compositing module, and a BEV feature loss that attacks internal representations rather than only final boxes.

The empirical study is fairly broad in the digital setting, covering BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer, transfer attacks, distance sensitivity, different mesh initializations, loss ablations, color-vs-geometry ablations, and a simple defense setting.

The reported drops are substantial. With realistic occlusion enabled, BEVDet mAP drops from 0.2754 for the benign inserted object to 0.1597 for the adversarial object, and similar degradation is shown for BEVDet4D and BEVFormer.
The paper makes a useful attempt to separate benign occlusion effects from adversarial effects by reporting Clean, Init, and Adv results, which is important for this threat model.
weaknesses: The realism of the threat model is weakened by substantial oracle information. Mesh placement uses target vehicle 3D annotations, and the occlusion module uses annotated scene objects plus SAM2 masks. This is acceptable for dataset-based robustness evaluation, but it undercuts claims of practical deployment unless the attacker can obtain comparable geometry and object information at test time.

The term “universal” is not fully convincing as presented. The object texture/geometry may be universal, but the evaluation appears to place one or more copies near target vehicles using ground-truth-dependent positions, and the supplement notes 15 meshes at test time. This makes the attack stronger than a single naturally placed physical object and should be separated more clearly.

The physical validation is only qualitative and uses a simplified sequential six-view capture setup with a single camera, manual/external reconstruction, and no quantitative detection metrics. This supports plausibility, but not the strong real-world effectiveness claims made in the abstract and conclusion.

The semantic/contextual vulnerability interpretation is overstated. Visual resemblance to pedestrians or traffic cones and induced false positives suggest possible context exploitation, but the paper does not provide controlled evidence that learned environmental priors, rather than local texture artifacts or detector feature sensitivity, are the dominant mechanism.

Baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying. Adv3D and UAP have different assumptions and deployment patterns, and the paper mostly argues conceptual differences rather than adapting baselines into a matched scene-level, multi-view, occlusion-aware evaluation. This limits the strength of comparative claims.

Some evaluation choices need clearer justification. ASR is defined as 1 - Nadv/Ninit over detected vehicles, but it is not always clear whether this measures per-target disappearance, scene-level count reduction, localization failure, or category-specific failures. The use of multiple meshes also makes scene-level mAP degradation harder to attribute to a single adversarial object.

Reproducibility is moderate but incomplete. The paper gives many implementation details, training times, mesh sizes, and losses, but exact placement policies, target sampling, optimization constraints, renderer settings, physical printing details, and whether code/assets will be released are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper studies an important and timely robustness problem for camera-based BEV 3D detectors, and the non-invasive 3D object threat model is more interesting than standard pixel/patch perturbations attached to target vehicles.

The proposed pipeline combines differentiable 3D rendering, multi-view consistency, an occlusion-aware compositing step, and BEV feature-level objectives. This is a reasonable technical construction for exploring spatially consistent adversarial objects.

The experimental section covers several representative BEV detectors on nuScenes, reports clean/init/adversarial performance, includes ablations over loss terms, geometry, placement distance, transfer, and a simple defense, and compares against related Adv3D/UAP-style baselines.

The distinction between the performance drop from a benign inserted object and the additional drop after optimization is useful, since it partially separates ordinary occlusion or clutter effects from adversarial effects.
The paper includes a physical proof-of-concept, which is valuable for a physical adversarial attack paper even if the evaluation is limited.
weaknesses: The threat model and evaluation rely heavily on privileged scene information. Mesh placement uses 3D annotations of target vehicles, and occlusion handling uses annotated scene objects plus SAM2 masks. This makes the attack closer to an offline dataset manipulation pipeline than a clearly deployable non-invasive real-world attack, weakening the central practicality claim.

The physical experiment is not strong enough to support the paper’s real-world claims. It is qualitative, apparently uses a single ZED2i camera moved sequentially to emulate six cameras, relies on calibrated/reconstructed extrinsics, and reports no quantitative real-world success rate, number of scenes, repetitions, lighting variation, or failure cases.

Several headline claims are over-interpreted. The paper repeatedly claims a “semantic vulnerability,” “over-reliance on contextual reasoning,” and “dataset deficiencies,” but the evidence is mostly detection degradation from optimized textures near vehicles. The work does not isolate semantic context from low-level texture artifacts, occlusion, detector feature perturbation, or distribution shift.

The comparison to baselines is not fully convincing. Adv3D and UAP operate under different threat models, object counts, occlusion assumptions, and target definitions; the paper itself acknowledges these differences but still draws strong superiority conclusions. The UAP comparison excludes the Real Occ setting and the Adv3D comparison appears affected by different initial object effects, so the evidence for superiority is limited.

The attack setting sometimes becomes impractical or internally inconsistent. The supplement states training uses 2-4 meshes per image while test uses 15 meshes, and placement generalization uses guaranteed-visible random meshes without Real Occ. These choices inflate attack strength while moving away from the claimed realistic deployment setting.

The occlusion model is only approximate and may not guarantee physical realism. The BEV convex-hull visibility check plus 2D overlap does not fully resolve depth ordering or fine geometry, and SAM2 mask quality is not evaluated. Errors in this module could materially affect both attack visibility and claimed realism.

The optimization and loss definitions are underspecified or unclear in places. For example, the target region mapping to confidence space, how predicted boxes are matched for the localization loss, which BEV feature layer is used, and how gradients propagate through the occlusion/SAM step are not described sufficiently for confident reproduction.

The ASR metric and interpretation need more care. ASR increases as the IoU threshold becomes stricter in several tables, which may follow from the definition but makes it hard to distinguish missed detections from localization degradation. The paper should report standard nuScenes detection breakdowns and target-specific recall/precision more transparently.

Reproducibility is limited. Important implementation details are scattered across the supplement, but code availability, exact detector checkpoints/configs, mesh assets, optimization schedules beyond a few hyperparameters, physical printing details, and randomization protocols are insufficiently specified.

The presentation has notable polish issues, including grammar errors, awkward phrasing, inconsistent terminology, and some confusing table/figure descriptions. These are secondary to the technical concerns, but they add friction when assessing an already complex attack setup.

strengths: The paper proposes a timely and useful threat model for camera-based BEV 3D detection: non-invasive, universal 3D adversarial objects placed in the environment rather than on the target vehicle. This is meaningfully distinct from target-mounted camouflage and 2D patch attacks.

The method is technically coherent. Mesh placement in calibrated 3D scenes, differentiable rendering, explicit occlusion handling, and BEV feature-level scene confusion form a plausible pipeline for multi-view and temporal consistency.

The experimental evaluation is broad for this type of robustness work. The paper reports nuScenes results on BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer, and GeoBEV; comparisons to Adv3D and UAP; ablations over shape, distance, loss terms, color versus geometry; transfer attacks; a simple robust-model evaluation; and proof-of-concept physical experiments.

The reported attack effects are substantial and are separated from benign object insertion effects. For example, with realistic occlusion enabled, BEVDet drops from 0.3682 Init NDS to 0.2668 Adv NDS, and analogous drops appear for BEVDet4D and BEVFormer.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, including mesh sizes, optimization settings, training cost, physical data acquisition, print-aware optimization, transfer results, and additional metrics, which improves confidence in the empirical claims.
weaknesses: Some of the strongest interpretive claims are under-supported. The paper repeatedly argues that the attack reveals deep contextual reasoning failures, semantic co-occurrence bias, and dataset deficiencies, but these conclusions are mostly inferred from attack success and texture appearance rather than tested through controlled semantic/context experiments.

Comparisons to prior methods are informative but not fully clean because the threat models differ substantially. Adv3D, UAP, and SABER vary in invasiveness, placement, target selection, occlusion, and evaluation setup, so claims of superiority should be stated more cautiously.

The physical validation is promising but limited. It appears mostly qualitative and uses an emulated six-camera setup with sequential captures rather than a full synchronized vehicle-mounted system. There is limited statistical evaluation across lighting, distances, vehicle types, locations, and repeated trials.

The occlusion and realism model remains approximate despite being better than naive rendering. It depends on annotations and SAM2 masks and does not fully model lighting, shadows, reflective materials, full scene geometry, sensor pipelines, or print/display color shifts, all of which matter for physical plausibility.

Reproducibility is moderate rather than strong. The paper gives many details, but the attack depends on detector internals, SAM2, PyTorch3D, exact checkpoints, scene selection, mesh placement heuristics, and large compute. The manuscript does not make clear whether code, trained meshes, and exact protocols will be released.

The evaluation is still concentrated on nuScenes and a small family of BEV detectors. The general claim that current BEV perception systems share this vulnerability would be stronger with additional datasets, more recent architectures, and stronger or more targeted defense baselines.
